analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal milk price floor and limits how much overproducing dairy farms can sell at full support prices.
analysis.headline: Sole-sponsored and never granted a committee vote, the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended; seven weeks in, the House had already pointed dairy work to a separate bill.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the government's milk price support from $10.10 to $12.60 per hundredweight, guaranteeing dairy farmers a roughly 25% higher floor price. To keep surpluses in check, it creates a two-tier system: each farm gets a production base from its sales history, and milk sold above that base earns only $5.00 per hundredweight, with the difference paid back to the government. It also requires that all beverage milk, lowfat milk, and skim milk contain minimum levels of milk solids.
analysis.who_benefits: Dairy farmers, particularly those selling within their assigned production base, would receive a substantially higher guaranteed price for their milk. Milk producers also gain from the requirement that beverage milk contain more milk solids, which increases the amount of milk used per carton sold.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Dairy farmers within their production bases

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum federal milk price support from $10.10 to $12.60 per hundredweight, lifting the floor price processors must pay dairy farmers.

Creates a two-tier program that kicks in whenever the Agriculture Department estimates government purchases of surplus dairy will exceed 4.5 billion pounds: farms may sell up to their individual production base at the full support price, with base amounts set from each farm's sales history and adjusted to match national demand.
Lets dairy farmers transfer their production base only within a family or partnership, preserving the value of the base for existing farm families rather than opening it to buyers.
Requires beverage milk, lowfat milk, and skim milk to contain minimum milk solids, increasing the amount of milk used in each carton sold to consumers.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay more for milk, cheese, and other dairy products because the government-supported floor price rises about 25%. Taxpayers would fund larger government purchases of surplus dairy at the higher price in years when production stays high, though the two-tier penalty on over-base milk is designed to shrink those surpluses. Farms that want to expand, and brand-new dairy farmers, would take a steep price cut — about $5.00 per hundredweight — on all milk sold above their historical base.
analysis.who_pays_short: Milk consumers, taxpayers, and expanding farms

drawbacks.text: A 25% higher support floor is paid for at the grocery store: consumers would face higher prices for milk, cheese, butter, and other dairy staples.

Farms expanding production and new farmers entering the business would receive only $5.00 per hundredweight for milk sold above their historical base — far below the cost of production — which discourages growth and entry even in a year when demand is strong.
The solids-content mandates would force changes to how lowfat and skim milk are formulated, adding cost to milk processing that is likely passed on to shoppers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a large, direct income boost to dairy farmers paid for by a broad, diffuse cost — higher dairy prices for every household, plus taxpayer exposure to government surplus purchases. The two-tier design is a genuine attempt to limit overproduction and taxpayer cost, but the base system's steep penalty on over-base milk works against expanding and new farms. On balance this is a transfer to a concentrated producer interest rather than a policy with broad public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and its dairy subcommittee and never advanced to a markup or a floor vote; seven weeks after introduction the House noted that further action should be sought in a separate dairy bill, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Collin Peterson of Minnesota introduced the Dairy Stabilization Act of 1991 on May 21, 1991, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee on the day of introduction, then to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry a week later, and requested the Agriculture Department's view.

On July 9, 1991 — seven weeks after introduction — the House action record pointed further consideration to a separate bill, H.R. 2837, and H.R. 2417 itself received no markup, no vote, and no further action.
The bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, without ever coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Milk drinkers and taxpayers came out ahead, since the higher milk price floor and the solids mandates never took effect. Dairy farmers gained nothing from the bill's death, though the separate 1991 dairy legislation became the vehicle for industry policy instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Milk drinkers and taxpayers; dairy farmers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Collin C. Peterson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Agriculture Committee; it drew no cosponsors.

for.name: House Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry
for.role: House Agriculture subcommittee with jurisdiction over dairy policy
for.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 28, 1991, and requested the Agriculture Department's comments; no markup followed.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee from May 21, 1991 onward; it never received a markup or a vote, and on July 9 the record pointed further action to H.R. 2837 instead.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew no cosponsors, so its support never took a visible partisan shape; it came from a Minnesota dairy-district Democrat and was referred to a committee then chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill raises their guaranteed floor price about 25%, paid for through higher retail dairy prices and larger government purchases of surplus milk. The two-tier base shields existing producers while sharply penalizing farms that expand or enter the business.

industries.industry: Dairy processors and beverage milk handlers
industries.note: Processors would owe higher minimum milk prices and would have to collect and remit the $5.00-per-hundredweight assessment on over-base milk to the government. The solids-content mandates would force costlier formulations for lowfat and skim milk, costs typically passed to shoppers.

A higher support price would increase the cost of government dairy purchases in surplus years, but the two-tier program is designed to shrink those surpluses by capping how much over-base milk earns full price. The net fiscal effect depends on how strongly the base limits production.
